Adults disappear before the end of the rainy season and are not seen again until the next rainy season. Juveniles can be found in forests and at forest edges, suggesting that the species is a forest dweller rather than living in open environments (Roberto et al. 2014).

Up to 34 prey items were found in the stomachs of R. casconi specimens and composed mostly of ants (70%) and beetles (11%). Other arthorpods also found in the stomachs included species from the orders Diptera, Orthoptera, Hemiptera, Isoptera, Aranea, and Acari (Roberto et al. 2014).
trends_and_threats: The species authorities of Rhinella casconi recommend the species be listed as "Vulnerable B1 ab (iii, iv)" because of its small range size and fragmented habitat. Like many other species in the Serra de Baturité mountain range, it is threatened by habitat loss due to deforestation for human settlements and banana plantations (Roberto et al. 2014).

description:
B. chavin is characterized by having large, elevated, elongate glands on each forearm and tibia, two large, elevated, elongate glands on the outer dorsal margin of each foot and aone small, elevated gland on the outer dorsal margin of each hand. Snout-vent lengths ranged from 54.8 to 64.9 mm for females and from 47.5 to 52.0 mm for males.
Individuals exhibit considerable color variation. The dorsal and lateral ground color ranges from shades of brown to green with brown, grey, green or white spotting. The throat, chest, venter, and extremities are sulphur-yellow, cream, light brown or grey with dark brown, dark grey and white blotches and spots. The ventral surfaces of the hands and feet are olive-brown or chestnut. Some have a middorsal line.
distribution: B. chavin was collected from two cloud forest localities, at 3010 and 3017 m, from the eastern Andean slopes of central Peru. These localities are described as "bosques framentados", or naturally fragmented forests.
life_history: Eggs are relatively large, yolky, and unpigmented.  It has been suggested that breeding occurs in the rainy season, the end of August through the end of March.

common_name: Chullachaki Beaked Toad, Sapo picudo Chullachaki (Spanish)

comments:
In 2021, Pereyra et al. reviewed the entire genus Rhinella presenting comprehensive datasets in a phylogenetic analysis. By implication from several previous works, Rhinella diptycha includes the synonyms: Rhinella jimi (Pereyra et al. 2021), Rhinella schneideri (Chaparro et al 2007), Bufo pisanoi (Casamiquela 1967); but see Amphibian Species of the World for complete bibliography (link at top left).

This species was featured in News of the Week October 18, 2021:

Amphibians are known for their very permeable skin that functions in gas and water exchange. Frogs, in particular, have colonized very dry habitats worldwide that would create seemingly conflict between the need for oxygen uptake (required for metabolism) and water loss (potential desiccation). To better understand how frogs, and especially their skin, cope with dry habitats, Mailho-Fontana et al. (2021) compared the skin, physiology, and behavior of two closely related toad species, the Yellow Cururu Toad and Cope's Toad (Rhinella icterica and R. jimi, which is now known as R. diptycha, respectively) that experience different climates. The authors found that the Cope's Toad from drier climate regions had thicker and more glandular skin, showed lower rates of water loss and displayed stereotyped behaviors to increase water uptake when dehydrated. These findings link differences in form, function, and behavior to illuminate strategies for desiccation resistance in frogs. (MWomack)
description:
[Description originally from Rhinella jimi, now a synonym of R. diptycha (Pereyra et al. 2021).]

This is a large, stout toad with a snout-vent length of approximately 147 mm (standard deviation of 16.34) in males and 134 mm (standard deviation of 29.71) in females. The body of is wider than long, with a rounded snout when viewed from the side and exhibits a semicircular shape when viewed ventrally. The head is very wide and has thick and discernible cranial crests. The cranial crest on the snout is similarly thick and somewhat projected from the snout. The nostrils are protuberant and directed posteriorly towards the back of the head. There are short, thick arcs above the lips. The canthal ridge is distinct, and the loreal region protrudes slightly. The eyelids are thick with projected edges and keratinized spines along the edges. It has a distinctly rounded tympanum with a few keratinized points. There are parotoid glands behind the supra-tympanic crests; these crests are broad when viewed from the front but are slender when viewed from behind. Elongated tubercles are situated behind each parotoid gland, and these tubercles reach to the median inguinal region. The dorsal surface has many tubercles of varying sizes, and there are keratinized spines on the skin. On males, these points have small spines and make the skin feel similar to sandpaper; females do not have these spines and feels smoother. There are two visible clusters of glands on both sides of the cloaca that are present on every individual. Males have strong, somewhat wide arms, whereas females have slimmer arms. This species has well-defined forearm glands when viewed dorsally. They have rounded inner metacarpal tubercles. The larger outer metacarpal tubercle is also rounded, and followed by a line of smaller, slightly keratinized tubercles along the ventral surface of the forearms. The species has no finger webbing, and their relative lengths are as follows: III > IV > I > II. The fingers have divided subarticular tubercles. The legs are short and thick with hard-to-define, irregular tibiae glands. The metatarsal fold is low, thick, and covered by a line of keratinized points. The feet are longer than wide with an oval-shaped inner metatarsal tubercle. The feet have a main, well-defined gland that reaches to the fifth toe when viewed from the side; in addition, there’s a less-defined gland within the metatarsal region. The toes are webbed proximally, but are distally fringed. The toe lengths are as follows: IV > III > V > II > I. The singular subarticular tubercles are small and rounded (Stevaux 2002).

Rhinella icterica does not have the tibial glands that R. diptycha does, but they share similar osteological, reproductive, and morphological traits. Rhinella marina and R. poeppigii represent a more basal clade, and, along with R. rubescens and R. arenarum, have smaller parotoid glands and more elongated skulls (Stevaux 2002).

In preservation, the dorsum of R. diptycha is a grayish-beige and dappled with almost-symmetrical dark brown spots from the parotoid glands to the posterior region on both sides of the body. The parotoid glands appear orange. While most of the body is beige, the ventral surface is lighter than the dorsum. The head is very dark, and is almost black in some individuals. Brown spots are more concentrated around the head and are scarcely present along the back (Stevaux 2002).

The species displays sexual dimorphism. Males have spines on the keratinized spikes on their skin, while females do not. This is most evident in the smoother skin texture of females (Stevaux 2002).

In the original description of Rhinella jimi, Stevaux (2002) noted that it is likely a species within the Rhinella schneideri species complex, which is largely distributed around South America. Rhinella jimi is sympatric with R. schneideri in the northeastern region of Brazil, but they clearly represent differentiated species. Because both R. jimi and R. schneideri both have tibial glands and a similar parotoid gland shape, implying a close phylogenetic relationship. However, R. jimi has a forearm gland, an external gland on its feet, and gland conglomerates on either side of its cloaca, all of which are absent in R. schneideri. Rhinella jimi has slightly shorter eyelids, a smaller eye diameter, smaller hands, and a slightly larger metatarsal fold length (Stevaux 2002).
distribution: Rhinella diptycha can be found across the entire northeastern region of Brazil at low altitudes (from sea level to 500 m). Rhinella diptycha has been specifically found between the State of Maranhão to the State of Bahia. The species can be found in the northern rainforest areas along the Atlantic coast, in the areas of caatinga (a type of vegetation found in deserts) in Maracás, and in the dry areas of Cabaceiras in Paraíba (Stevaux 2002).
editedby: Ann T. Chang, Michelle S. Koo
life_history:
As R. jimi, Rhinella diptycha is reported to breed in both permanent and temporary ponds (Andrade and Carnaval 2004).

Rhinella diptycha stores bufotoxins in its parotoid glands; when ingested, these toxins can cause paralysis, tremors, and death in predators. One of the main predators is Athene cunicularia, a burrowing owl that can be found in North and South America. Because there have been few other observed predators of Cope's Toad, it is thought that its bufotoxins are an effective defensive mechanism (Protázio et. al 2011).
trends_and_threats:
The current IUCN status of Rhinella diptycha is “Data Deficient” and the IUCN status lists no current threats to this species (Andrade and Carnaval 2004; Scott et al 2004). However, one danger facing its synonymized Rhinella jimi population is railroad collisions. Railroad segments pass through the Amazon in Brazil, but it is otherwise an undisturbed landscape. Researchers found a variety of toad carcasses along the railroad tracks, including R. jimi. While some of the individuals died from direct train collisions, others were killed by barotrauma. Barotrauma occurs when moving trains quickly change the air pressure around the toad, pushing air against them and fatally pushing their stomachs through their mouths. Some smaller toad carcasses were found dried out along the tracks. This is likely due to their inability to cross the tracks and find a suitably moist shelter. Toads are most vulnerable to railroad deaths during their migration period between the dry and wet seasons. The researchers found that railroads result in over 10,000 railroad fatalities annually (Dornas et al. 2019).

Current conservation efforts in Brazil include designated conservation sites and protected areas of R. diptycha's habitats (Andrade and Carnaval 2004).

comments: Juveniles of Bufo marinus are similar in general form and color to B. granulosus, but B. marinus has distinct parotoid glands behind the eyes, whereas the parotoid glands of B. granulosus are smaller and difficult to see in juveniles.
description: Males 60-70 mm, females 80-90 mm. The dorsum is granular in texture, and the dorsal coloration has a background of various shades of brown with irregular darker patches. The species has parotoid glands posterior to the eyes, but they are not very distinct. The belly is whitish to cream. The throat region of males is greenish yellow in the reproductive season.
distribution: The species is most often found on the edges of the Reserva Florestal Adolpho Ducke in Brazil and in large open areas.
life_history: The species is terrestrial and nocturnal. In the Reserva Florestal Adolpho Ducke in Brazil, it reproduces in small and large ponds throughout the year, but with a peak in the wet season. Clutches contain around 900 eggs that are deposited on the surface of the water in gelatinous strings. The tadpoles are light gray and live on the bottom of ponds.

comments: Rhinella humboldti belongs to the Rhinella granulosa species group and was first described by Gallardo (1965) as a subspecies. Later, the population from Trinidad and the Orinoco basin described as R. beebei was synonymized with R. humboldti. More recently, Murphy et al. (2017), based on molecular, morphological and bioacoustic evidence, suggested that R. beebei and R. humboldti are distinct species separated by the Eastern Cordillera of Colombia and Cordillera of Merida in Venezuela. The molecular information was from 12s and 16s mtDNA and Maximum Likelihood and Bayesian methods were used to analyze the data.
description:
Rhinella humboldti is a South American toad in which females have a snout-vent length range of 33.7 - 70.4 mm and males have a snout-vent length range of 32.5 - 64.4 mm. The head is wider than long. The snout is rounded in the dorsal and lateral views, and is longer than wide. The nostril shape is subelliptic, located closer to the tip of the snout than to the eye. The canthus rostralis is slightly angulated. The eyes are laterally located and their diameter is shorter than the distance between the eyes, but longer than the distance between the eye and the nostril. The ocular crests are smooth. The tympanum is taller than wide with visible borders close to the postorbital crest. The cranial crests are mostly continuous and serrate (wrinkled), the crest above the tympanum is long and granulose. Parietal crests are inconspicuous or almost absent, sub-nasal crest long reaching beyond posterior margin of the nostril, sometimes in contact with preorbital crest. Paratoid glands on the shoulders are longer than tall (the width of paratoid glands are 12.3 - 21.7% of the snout-vent length; the height is 10 - 17.8% of the snout-vent length), with a subtriangular shape but with conspicuous vertex pointing down. The relative finger lengths are II < I < IV < III without interdigital membranes. Presence of nuptial rough pads on the dorsum of finger I and II. Relative toe sizes are I < II < V < III < IV with interdigital membranes with serrate borders that do not contact the tip of the toes following the formula 1 - 2 II 1 - 3 III 2 - 3½ IV 3½+ - 1 V (Gallardo 1965, Narvaes and Rodriguez 2009). For more description, see Narvaes and Rodriguez (2009).

Diagnosis:

Compared to R. humboldti, the cephalic crests of R. granulosa are granulose, with low supraorbital crest and less developed maxillary crest. Rhinella pygmaea, R. bergi, and R. azarai are smaller, with mean snout-vent length in males being 32.1 mm, 40.4 mm, 42.1 mm, respectively and females being 40.8 mm, 49.9 mm, 45.4 mm, respectively (conversely, male snout-vent length is 46.6 mm, and 52.2 mm in female R. humboldti). Additionally, the cephalic crests in the three species are always continuous, and parietal crests are present. In R. major the snout is straight (not rounded or pointy) in lateral view and squared in dorsal view (rounded in R. humboldti), the interorbital area has just a few granules or is absent, and the maxillary crest and labial light stripe are visible in dorsal view. In R. dorbignyi and R. fernandezae the snout is shorter in lateral and dorsal views (snout longer than wide in R. humboldti), the parotoid glands are smaller, the postorbital space is larger, and the posterior margin of nostril does not surpass anterior margin of mandible in lateral view. Rhinella mirandaribeiroi has a longitudinal, mid-dorsal stripe, elongated head, dorsoventrally flattened snout, and less developed maxillary crest (maxillary crests project in front of the mandible in R. humboldti). Rhinella nattereri can be distinguished from R. humboldti by its rounded head with long snout, squared snout in dorsal view, shorter sub-nasal crest, and having its posterior portion not extending beyond posterior margin of nostril. Rhinella merianae has a shorter and wider head, squared snout in dorsal view that is narrower and sloping dorsoventrally. Rhinella centralis shows a high concentration of small keratinized granules on top of head, and a narrower snout that leans both dorsally and ventrally. Rhinella beebei has beaded ocular crests versus the smooth ocular crests in R. humboldti (Murphy et al. 2017, Narvaes and Rodriguez 2009).

Coloration:

In life, R. humboldti has cryptic coloration without a mid-dorsal, longitudinal stripe. The dorsum is usually brown with large black spots. The limbs with traverse black bands, and the belly usually with light yellow pigment (Gallardo 1965, Narvaes and Rodriguez 2009). For more coloration, see Narvaes and Rodriguez (2009).

Variation:

A few males possess nuptial pads on the lateral surface of finger III. Certain individuals possess a long but inconspicuous infraorbital crest, extending beyond the postorbital crest. Specimens from Isla Margarita in Venezuela usually have keratinized branches from the cephalic crest covering the interorbital area. In Trinidad and Tobago, specimens are slightly smaller in snout-vent length, where males average 42.2 mm and females average 51.5 mm, compared to individuals from the continent, where males average 46.6 mm and females average 52.2 mm (Narvaes and Rodrigues 2009).
distribution: Rhinella humboldti is found west of the Eastern Cordillera along the Magdalena River to the Caribbean coast in Colombia and northwest of the Cordillera of Merida, Venezuela (Gallardo 1965, IUCN 2023, Narvaes and Rodrigues 2009). Initially, when R. beebei was considered conspecific to R. humboldti, the latter had a cis-Andean distribution, as well, but Murphy et al. (2017) restored R. beebei as a valid species, restricting R. humboldti to a trans-Andean distribution. Rhinella humboldti is mainly found at lower elevations up to a maximum of 1000 m (IUCN 2023). Note, the Central American populations are now recognized as R. centralis (Narvaes and Rodrigues 2009).
larva:
Lynch (2006) provided a description of R. humboldti tadpoles from the northern lowlands of Colombia (reported as Bufo granulosus). The oral disc has marginal labial papillae with an obvious dorsal and posterior gap.

Tadpoles of R. humboldti (reported as Bufo granulosus) can be distinguished from R. marinus (reported as Bufo marinus) by color pattern; R. marina is bicolored, dark dorsally with cream color ventrally, while R. humboldti bears dark saddles on the caudal musculature (Lynch 2006).
life_history:
Rhinella humboldti is a terrestrial species that can be found hidden under rocks and fallen logs or in holes during the day and has been reported in open field plantations during the night (Renjifo and Lundberg 1999).

The advertisement call resembles the structure of the call in other species of the R. granulosa species group. The mean number of notes per call is 100.3 ± 27.1 (49 – 145 notes). The duration of each note is 0.022 s ± 0.001 (0.021 – 0.023 s), with an inter-note gap of 0.009 s ± 0.001 (0.008 – 0.011 s). Four pulses per note are consistent for all calls, and the mean pulse duration is 0.004 s ± 0.000 (0.003 – 0.004 s). The interpulse duration is constant across calls at 0.002 s (Torres-Suárez and Vargas-Salinas 2013).

Eggs are laid in lentic water bodies (Triana et al. 2013).

Despite the presence of bufotoxins, R. humboldti are apparently prey for several larger vertebrate predators. Miller (1947) collected a Savanna Hawk (reported as Heterospizias meridionalis meridionalis, now Buteogallus meridionalis) near the Tatacoa Desert (Upper Magdalena Valley) containing the “remains of about six small toads” in the gullet, which were identified as Bufo granulosus (now R. humboldti) by Stebbins and Hendrickson (1959) who inferred that the hawk was “working the wetlands for toads.” Vargas-Salinas and Aponte-Gutierrez (2013) reported a cat-eyed snake (Leptodeira septentrionalis) attempted to prey on a R. humboldti in the middle Magdalena Valley, Colombia, from which the toad managed to escape by puffing up its body and applying resistance with one of its hind legs, there is still no evidence on the use of defensive cutaneous toxins secretions, but it is still not discarded as part of the strategy to avoid predation (Vargas-Salinas and Aponte-Gutierrez 2013). Additionally, frogs from the genus Leptodactylus possess genes that confer resistance to toad toxins making R. humboldti a possible prey item (Mohammadi et al. 2021).

Adult R. humboldti are likely generalist predators feeding mainly on insects and other terrestrial invertebrates according to feeding behavior of other toad species of the genus (Batista et al. 2011, Fajardo Martinez et al. 2013, Sampedro-Marín et al. 2011, Zug and Zug 1979).
trends_and_threats: Rhinella humboldti is catalogued as “Least Concern” (IUCN 2023). However, it is often found in areas with human settlement and agriculture, and there is evidence of moderate detrimental effects of the pesticide glyphosate on development and mortality of embryos. Using the suggested concentrations of the pesticide to spread on a hectare (2376.96 μL per liter) caused almost 18% mortality of the embryos (Triana et al. 2013).

comments:
Toads from the Eldorado locality, in Misiones, near the Paraná borders, show remarkable morphological peculiarities, with characters both of Rhinella (Bufo) schneideri, as the shape of the dorsal warts or the presence of tibial glands, and of Rhinella ictericus, as the parotoid shape or the dorsal pattern. More available biological data are needed to make clear the identity of such a mixed or intermediate population.

This species was featured in News of the Week 14 August 2023:
Amphibians are found across a wide range of elevations, from sea level to above 5,000 meters, exposing them to a wide range of climates. The climate variability hypothesis predicts that organisms exposed to more temperate variation will be able to function across a wider range of temperatures. Bovo et al. (2023) tested the thermal tolerances of five species of frogs that are distributed across mountains in Brazil's Atlantic Rainforest in a variety of microhabitats, including Boana faber, Dendropsophus minutus, Leptodactylus latrans, Physalaemus cuvieri, and Rhinella icterica. They found differences among species in temperature tolerance, but did not always find that broader temperature variation at increasing elevations correlated with broader temperature tolerance. In addition, they did not find a consistent difference in water loss or water uptake across altitude or climates. Overall, they did not find strong support for the climate variability hypothesis or for elevation shaping these physiological traits. (MWomack)
description: A large robust toad (adult male :100-166 mm;  adult female : 135-190 mm). Body stout; strong cephalic crests and large parotoid glands on head. Tympanum small, higher than wide. Skin of dorsum scattered with blunt thorny warts, especially in males;  dorsum yellowish in females and juveniles with a regular pattern of black blotches and a wide light-colored middorsal stripe. The color of the male dorsum is often a bright greenish yellow with only a few black blotches; belly white, marbled with brown.
distribution: The rain forest (Mata Atlântica) of southeastern and southern Brazil, eastern Paraguay, and also in Misiones (Argentina). Usually in elevated forests, also in grassland. During breeding time, they are found in streams and standing water bodies, such as lakes, ponds or puddles.
life_history: Spawning period from August to January. In November and December hundreds of the diurnal, only 9-10 mm sized, recently metamorphosed froglets leave the breeding places en mass. Males call in and at water bodies, mainly at night but also during the day. The call is a melodious tremolo (pointed out by the indigenous name “Cururu”). The large egg strings with several thousand dark-colored eggs are deposited at shallow water. The small, black, free-swimming larvae live in large congregations, feeding on suspension and grazing on stones and aquatic plants. Most of adult toads are “Sit-and-Wait-Predators” feeding on invertebrates especially Coleoptera and Formicidae.

comments:
Rhinella kuka was previously thought to be R. fissipes. Maximum Likelihood analysis of mitochondrial 16S rRNA found that R. kuka is a distinct species and is a member of the R. veraguensis species group. Members of the group included in this analysis were R. justiniano, R. inca, R. leptoscelis, R. quechua, R. rumbolli and R. veraguensis. From those, the most closely related species is R. rumbolli, however, this relationship is not strongly supported (Köhler et al. 2023). Members of the R. veraguensis species group include: R chrysophora (possibly extinct), R. fissipes, R. gnustae, R. inca, R. justinianoi, R. leptoscelis, R. quechua (which includes specimens labeled as R. amboroensis), R. rumbolli, and R. veraguensis (Pereyra et al. 2021, Köhler et al. 2023).

Rhinella kuka was previously called Bufo fissipes, Rhinella fissipes, and Rhinella leptoscelis (Köhler et al. 2023).

The description of this species is based on museum specimens collected in 1998 and 1999 (Köhler et al. 2023).
description:
Rhinella kuka is a large toad that was described from five females, one male and one juvenile with a snout to vent length range in females of 66 - 72 mm and the male being 62.8 mm. The head is wider than long but narrower than the body. From the dorsal view, the head is triangular. The short snout is subacuminate without a bulbous tip in the dorsal view and rounded when viewed from the profile. The mandibular angle of the jaw protrudes in the dorsal view and has a few enlarged, lateral subconical tubercles. The protuberant, medium-sized, rounded nostrils are much closer to the snout tip than the eyes, located approximately at the anterior margin of the jaw, and are directed laterally. The internarial area is concave. The canthus rostralis has a sharp, angular, elevated ridge that is slightly convex in the dorsal view. The loreal region is concave. The eye diameter is greater than the eye to nostril distance but less than the internal distance. The upper eyelid protrudes, is strongly granular with low tubercles, and thickens laterally above the eye. There are several crests around the eye and to the parotoid glands. A swollen canthal crest is present at the anterodorsal corner of the eye along with a slightly thick preorbital crest. There are also distinct supraorbital, and postorbital crests that are continuous. While there is no suborbital crest, an elevated and distinct occipital crest extends from the posterior of the eye to the parotoid gland. A short pretympanic crest and distinct, but short supratympanic crest that barely extends to the posterior margin of the tympanum are also present. Its tympanum is one and a half times greater in size than its eye diameter. The tympanic annulus is weakly developed and the posterior end is covered in thick skin. The distinct tympanic membrane is rounded, slightly taller than wide. Its relatively large parotoid glands have a subtriangular shape with rounded corners in both the dorsal and lateral view. The length of the parotid gland is about twice that of the eye diameter. The skull is hyperossified and there are eight presacral vertebrae. The dorsal skin on the head is relatively smooth with a few flat tubercles, however the dorsum is tuberculated with rounded, flat tubercles that are unevenly distributed and prominent, conical tubercles with keratinized tips. On the dorsolateral surface, the species also has enlarged, conical tubercles running continuously from the parotoid gland to the groin. The skin on the flanks has a dense scattering of keratinized, conical tubercles. The dorsal surfaces of the forelimbs and hind limbs are spiculated with dense, subconical tubercles. The ventrum of the species, including the throat and chest, is granular. The protruding cloacal opening is positioned at the upper level of the thighs and directed posteriorly. There is no cloacal sheath present. The slender forelimb is long, with the forearm being almost a quarter of the snout-vent length. The prominent palmar tubercle is elevated and ellipsoid. The thenar tubercle is smaller and spade-like. The long, slender fingers have a slight trace of fleshy, basal webbing, well-defined serrated lateral fringes, relative finger length of II < I < IV < III, and end in round tips that are the same width as the fingers. The prominent subarticular tubercles of the fingers are round to slightly triangular and the obvious supernumerary tubercles are round. The slender hind limbs are moderately long with the tibia being slightly less than half the snout-vent length. The foot is only slightly shorter than the tibia. There is no tarsal fold, but an elevated and serrated tarsal ridge is present on the inner tarsus. The slightly protuberant inner metatarsal tubercle is medium-sized and oval. The oval outer metatarsal tubercle is about half the size of the inner. The toes are more moderately webbed with a webbing formula of I 0+ – 1- II 0.5 – 2- III 1 – 2.5 IV 3 – 1- V. The toes also have serrated lateral fringes, a relative toe length of < II < V < III < IV, and have rounded ends that are the same width as their toes. Both the distinct subarticular tubercles of the toes and smaller supernumerary tubercles are ovoid (Köhler et al. 2023).

DIAGNOSIS:

Rhinella kuka can be differentiated from other similar species in the R. veraguensis group primarily from examination of its head, dorsal sublateral tubercles, vent coloration, legs, and phalanges. Its snout when viewed from the side is more rounded than R. fissipes, R. inca, and R. rumbolli. Its parotoid glands are more triangular and larger than those found on R. rumbolli and R. veraguensis. The presence of a tympanum larger than its eye also distinguishes it from R. chrysophora R. fissipes, R. justinianoi, R. rumbolli, and R. veraguensis. While similar species like R. gnustae, R. inca, and R. quechua either lack or have discontinuous dorsolateral tubercles, R. kuka has large dorsolateral tubercles from the parotoid gland to the groin. The focal species' cream colored vent distinguishes it from R. rumbolli and R. veraguensis, which have darker vents. Rhinella kuka generally has longer legs than similar species including R. fissipes, R. jusinianoi, and R. quechua. Rhinella kuka also has different finger size ordering than R. chrysophora, R. fissipes, and R. veraguensis. The presence of serrated fringes on the fingers and toes distinguishes R. kuka from R. gnustae, R. justinianoi, and R. veraguensis as well (Köhler et al. 2023).

COLORATION:

In life, R. kuka has reddish orange brown dorsal coloration with dark brown and black spots. A cream colored narrow stripe extends from its snout down its back along the vertebrae. Dark brown transverse stripes are found on the arms and legs. The ventral surface has a lighter background color than its dorsum, exhibiting orange, rusty brown, or pinkish tint. Its throat has densely packed small spots of dark brown. This dark flecked pattern is also found on the chest and vent. The tubercles on the hands and feet are cream colored, which contrasts with the brown coloration of the phalanges and limbs. Rhinella kuka has greenish bronze colored eyes (Köhler et al. 2023).

In preservative, the dorsum is a light brown color with nearly symmetrical dark brown markings and irregular flecks and blotches. The upper lip is cream with irregular, dark brown flecks. The interorbital area also had dark brown flecks. The loreal region is light brown. The parotoid glands are tan and the tympanum is brown. A narrow, pale vertebral stripe starts at the tip of the snout and extends to the cloaca. There are dark brown lines bordering the vertebral stripe between the scapula and sacrum. Along the dorsolateral edge is another narrow dark brown stripe that borders the dorsolateral row of tubercles. The flanks are tan and have a dense scattering of dark brown flecks and spots. The dorsal surfaces of the limbs have a tan background color with brown transverse bars. The ventral background color is yellowish-cream with the exception of the throat which is light brown with dark brown mottling and irregular spots. The chest and anterior venter also have dark brown mottled spots and a faint, Y-shaped creamed marking. The posterior region of the ventrum has a few scattered, dark brown spots or flecks. The ventral surface of the thighs also have a yellowish-cream background color with brown splotches. The posterior surfaces of the thighs are brown with darker brown marbling. The surfaces of the palms and planters are brown while the tubercles are cream (Köhler et al. 2023).

VARIATION:

The majority of the variation within the species appears to be in their coloration and patterning, however, there appears to also be mild sexual dimorphism. The variations in coloration and patterning include some specimens having more contrasting and complex patterns of cream, brown, dark brown and almost black areas as flecks, blotches, or spots on the dorsum. The brown stripes that border the cream colored vertebral stripe and the dark transversal bars on the upper surfaces of the limbs also vary in distinctiveness. Additionally, there is variation in how prominent the dark brown mottling and blotches on the throat, chest, and anterior venter are. Unlike the females, the male specimen has a uniform dorsal brown coloration, fewer dark spots, a cream color dorsolateral region. All R. kuka have a Y-shaped cream marking on the vent and chest, but there is variation in how distinctly the marking is exhibited. The juvenile specimen has more contrasting and sharper outlines. Sexual dimorphism is hard to assess as there was only one adult male specimen. However, females appear to have a more distinct continuous dorsolateral row of enlarged tubercles, and the male shows a mildly swollen cream-colored nuptial pad on his first finger (Köhler et al. 2023).
distribution: Rhinella kuka is found in Bolivia. It has been confirmed in the Carrasco National Park, located in Provincia Chapare, Departamento Cochabamba and the Isiboro Sécure National Park at the border between Departamentos Beni and Cochabamba. It is also likely that the species inhabits the Bolivian Yungas all the way into La Paz, but this has not been definitively confirmed. Their habitat mainly consists of montane rainforest with steep slopes and large amounts of rainfall (8000 mm/yr) with small streams running through it. Rhinella kuka can be found at elevations between 800 - 1650 m above sea level (Köhler et al. 2023).
larva: As of 2025, there is no information about the larval development or tadpole stage of Rhinella kuka (Köhler et al. 2023).
life_history:
Rhinella kuka is a terrestrial species, with individuals observed to be active at night on the ground, often on roads and roadside ditches during rainfall. The habitat lacks stagnant water bodies but contains numerous small streams (Köhler et al. 2023).

While the reproductive mode remains unknown, evidence suggests a prolonged reproductive period during the rainy season. This is based on observations of adult females who were collected in December, January, and February that contained eggs with a dark pole in their ovaries (Köhler et al. 2023).

There are no documented vocalizations for this species or any in the R. veraguensis group, leading to the assumption that they may be ‘voiceless’. However, a faint call recorded from R. leptoscelis by J.M. Padial and collaborators suggest that the species of the R. veraguensis group may discreetly communicate acoustically. It is also possible that they vocalize at times when herpetologists are less likely to be present, such as early in the morning (Köhler et al. 2023).

Sympatric bufonids in the Chapare region include Atelopus tricolor, suspected R. justinianoi, R. stanlanii, and R. veraguensis (Köhler et al. 2023).
trends_and_threats:
As of 2025, R. kuka has not been assessed by the IUCN Redlist of Threatened species, however, the authors proposed that R. kuka be categorized as “Vulnerable” under the IUCN Red List category (Köhler et al. 2023).

In an analysis of Bolivian amphibian diversity and conservation, De La Riva and Reichle (2014) found that habitat loss to deforestation and agriculture, water pollution, and chytridiomycosis were the main causes of amphibian declines in Bolivia. Chytridiomycosis, caused by Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, has been confirmed in R. quechua tadpoles, which are close in relation to R. kuka (Barrionuevo et al. 2008). Trombiculid mite infestations were also found in R. quechua (Wohltmann et al. 2006).

In order to protect the known locations of R. kuka, the Carrasco and Isiboro Sécure National Parks are working together to preserve the quality and extent of their habitat (Köhler et al. 2023).

comments: Maximum likelihood analysis was conducted using the 16S rRNA gene. The analysis found that R. kumanday is a member of the Rhinella festae species group, and that R. kumanday is sister to the clade consisting of R. paraguas, R. ruizi, and what is assumed to be R. nicefori (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).
common_name: Kumanday Beaked Toad (English), Sapo picudo del Kumanday (Spanish)
description:
Rhinella kumanday is a moderate-sized frog described from six females, two males, and a juvenile. Females have a snout-vent length ranging from 35.0 - 40.1 mm and the two males have snout-vent lengths of 36.4 mm and 37.8 mm. In the dorsal view, the head is triangular and in the lateral view the head is sharply protruding. The head is narrower than the body, and wider than it is long. The long snout is sharp, protruding, and anteroventrally directed. There is a sagittal ridge between the upper lip and the snout. The small nostrils are round and protuberant, located halfway between the tip of the snout and the anterior edge of the eye, and are not visible in the dorsal view. The canthus rostralis has a weak canthal crest and appears concave in the dorsal view. The loreal region is also concave. The diameter of the eye is greater than half the interorbital distance and greater than the distance between the eye and the nostril. There are small warts of varying shapes and sizes on the thick eyelid. There is no preorbital crest, but a supraorbital crest and weak postorbital crest can be found. There is no tympanic annulus or tympanic membrane. The well-developed oval to subtriangular parotid glands are large, about twice the eye diameter. The supratympanic crest is distinct and a parietal crest is present. Subconical warts with hard tips and minute, conical tubercles are present throughout the dorsal surface of the body. A dorsolateral row of subconical tubercles that extends from the parotoid gland toward the groin, forming a discontinuous fold, is often present. The skin on the flanks is granular with more prominent warts than the dorsum. The small, ovoid cloaca is located at the mid-level of the thighs and sticks out from the main body. The ventral skin on the belly has minute tubercles while the chest and gular are more granular. The forearm is slender and has a length that is about a quarter of the snout-vent length. The skin on the forearm is similar to the dorsum. The hand is long and slender and about equal in length to the forearm. The dorsal surface of the hand has dense minute tubercles. The palm has distinct small, ovoid palmar and thenar tubercles, with the thenar tubercle being less than half the size of the palmar tubercle. The rest of the palm has many warts, barely-visible minute tubercles, and diffuse supernumerary tubercles. Fingers are long, slender, with fringes along their sides and a relative finger length formula of I < II < IV < III. The basal finger webbing has a formula of I 1 – 2 II 1 – 2 III -2 – 2 IV or I 1 – 2 II 2 – 3 III -3 – 2+ IV. The fingertips are round and the subarticular tubercles are diffuse. Nuptial pads were not observed. The short, robust hind limbs have a slightly longer tibia than femur and foot. All three have a length that is about a third of the snout-vent length. The skin of the hind limbs is covered in warts and conical or subconical tubercles of varying size. They have tarsal folds, which is replaced by tubercles at the heel and merges with the postaxial lateral fringe on toe V. The inner metatarsal tubercle is round and three times larger than the barely visible, round outer metatarsal tubercle. The planter has flat warts, small accessory tubercles, and small, round supernumerary tubercles, which are all indistinct. Toes are long, slender, and contain fringes along their sides. The relative toe length is I < II < III < V < IV and the webbing formula of feet is I 0 – 0 II 0+ – 2- III 1 – 3- IV 3- –1+ V. Toe tips are round and the subarticular tubercles are round, diffuse, and barely discernable in some individuals (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

DIAGNOSIS:

Rhinella kumanday can be largely distinguished from other members of the Rhinella festae group by several characteristics. Its body is smaller than R. lindae, R. paraguas, R. tenrec, and R. truebae. Rhinella kumanday has a well-defined tarsal fold not seen in R. acrolopha, R. chullachaki, R. festae, R. lindae, R. macrorhina, R. nicefori, R. paraguas, R. rostrata, and R. truebae. Rhinella kumanday lacks a tympanum and annulus tympanic that is present in R. chavin, R. lilyrodriguezae, R. manu, R. multiverrucosa, R. nesiotes, R. tacana, and R. yanachaga. Rhinella kumanday can be further differentiated from R. acrolopha, R. festae, and R. macrorhina by its cranial crest being less prominent. Conversely, R. kumanday differs from R. paraguas by having a parietal crest, but lacking nuptial excrescences in males. And, R. kumanday has a prominent sagittal ridge located between the snout and upper lip that is absent in R. ruizi. In contrast to R. tenrec, the snout is not as sharp in R. kumanday, and the urostyle is fused to the sacrum. Lastly, R. kumanday has seven presacral vertebrae as opposed to eight in R. ruizi and R. tenrec (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

COLORATION:

In life, the dorsal surface of the head is brown with darker areas in the tympanum. The suborbital region is cream yellowish with lines that extend toward the mouth. The dorsal surface of the body is light brown, but there is high variation between individuals and dorsal coloration can range from light or dark brown to black (see variation two paragraphs below). Dark brown bands start above each eyelid and converge at a point in line with the parotid glands, making a V-shape, into a single, medial dorsal band then extending to the cloacal sheath. It is briefly disconnected at a region in line with the hind limbs, where the area is light brown instead. The flanks are light brown above but have a cream yellowish line with black spots below that extends from each upper eyelid over the parotoids to the groin. The lateral sides of limbs are light brown. The ventrum, posterior body, and extremities of the anterior region have a cream yellowish background. There are brown mottled marks that dominate the gular region but become more diffuse towards the belly. The vent is brown on the upper region with a few yellow spots but reversed as a yellow background with brown spots on the lower region. The tarsal fold is light yellow. The iris is golden with black mottled spots that are concentrated near the sclera and the pupil is circular (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

In preservative, the head becomes a darker brown. The suborbital region becomes mustard yellow. The flanks become dark brown, almost black, with a cream yellowish line with black spots that extends from each upper eyelid to the groin. The dorsal surfaces of the limbs are dark brown with cream yellowish webbing and tips of digits. The ventral surface remains similar to the coloration in life (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

VARIATION:

There is both minor sexual dimorphism and individual variation. Females have a greater eye-nostril distance and longer femurs. The tip of the head is pointed in females and blunt in males. Males lack nuptial excrescences and vocal slits. Individuals can vary in how continuous the dorsolateral row of tubercles is, with observations of scattered tubercles with no discernable row, a row starting just before the parotoids to ⅔ of the body, and a complete row from anterior to the parotoids to the groin. The dorsum can vary from light brown to darker brown to almost black. A cream or yellowish longitudinal line may be present on the dorsum. Brown mottling on the ventrum is highly variable. Other light cream lines may exist on the lateral part of the body (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).
distribution:
Rhinella kumanday is an endemic high-elevation toad from the Cordillera Central of the Colombian Andes, documented from the departments of Caldas (e.g., Manizales and Villamaría) and Quindío (e.g., Córdoba and Salento). Verified records indicate an elevational range of approximately 2404 - 3690 m a.s.l., with Quindío records around 2440 - 2460 m (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024; Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025). The Quindío localities extend the known distribution ~75 - 80 km south of the type locality region (Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025).

This species inhabits high-Andean Forest environments along the Cordillera Central. Individuals from the new localities were found in Andean secondary forest within a montane cloud-forest landscape characterized by high humidity and frequent fog, with surrounding habitat mosaics of native forest remnants, secondary forest, and agricultural lands (e.g., coffee cultivation). Records from forest fragments embedded in pastures suggest some tolerance of human-modified landscapes, although ongoing habitat alteration may pose risks (Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025).
larva: Not much is known about the larva of this species, though current findings suggest that it may be a direct developing species (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).
life_history:
Rhinella kumanday has been observed to be a largely terrestrial species that dwells among leaf litter and rotten logs on the forest floor near the edges of creeks and streams. However, microhabitat observations also include a male perched on vegetation roughly 50 cm above the ground in secondary forest. It exhibits crepuscular activity, meaning that it is mostly active during the early morning and twilight hours (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

Knowledge of the species' natural history and reproductive behavior remains incomplete. No tadpoles or amplectant pairs have been observed and attempts to record their calls in captivity have been unsuccessful. Ova in ovaries are described as large cream-yellow eggs that lack reticulations. While not much is known about their life history, the large concentration of yellowish cream yolk in their eggs indicates that this species has direct development. Other species within the Rhinella festae group, like R. manu, are also suspected to be directly developing (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

This species has been observed to exhibit thanatosis as a defensive behavior, feigning death upon discovery by a predator (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

The only known natural predator of R. kumanday is the False-Coral snake, Erythrolamprus lamonae (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

Based on the stomach contents of several specimens, R. kumanday are known to be insectivores, feeding on small invertebrates such as beetles, weevils, ticks, and mites (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).

Rhinella kumanday has a geographic range overlap with Osornophryne percrassa and Atelopus quimbaya (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024).
relation_to_humans: There are currently no published reports indicating that R. kumanday is consumed as food, used in traditional medicine, or collected for the pet trade. Available species descriptions and distribution-focused publications do not mention direct exploitation by local people. Human interactions appear to be primarily through scientific research and conservation planning, where the species is treated as a locally endemic component of Andean cloud-forest biodiversity (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024; Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025).
trends_and_threats:
Field surveys report low encounter rates and irregular temporal occurrence, suggesting R. kumanday may be naturally rare. However, population trends remain unknown due to limited data. Initially, its known records were clustered within a small portion of the Central Andes, and the restricted distribution has led authors to suggest the species could meet an “Endangered” category under IUCN criteria (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024), however its later presence approximately 75 – 80 km south of the historical localities suggest its threat status may be downgraded to “Vulnerable” (Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025).

Some subpopulations occur within protected areas (e.g., Parque Nacional Natural Los Nevados and Reserva Forestal Protectora Bosques de la CHEC). Newly discovered populations were found in a matrix of primary and secondary forest and agricultural land, which indicates the species may be tolerant of some human modifications. Potential threats include habitat fragmentation and degradation associated with current or proposed mining and other development projects in the region (Caicedo-Martínez et al. 2024; Mejía-Zuluaga et al. 2025).

description:
A medium sized species of the Bufo (Rhinella) margaritifera species group. (1) SVL of females 43.7 +/- 0.8 mm, of males 34.6 +/- 4.3 mm; (2) bony knob at angle of jaws absent, corner of mouth angular; (3) canthus rostralis smooth, concave laterally, without crests; (4) heel not reaching posterior margin of eye when hindlimbs adpressed; (5) cephalic crests low; (6) neural spines indistinct; (7) tympanum large but smaller than eye diameter, round in males, ovoid in females; (8) parotoid glands relatively small, elongated posteriorly; (9) upper eyelid without projections; (10) toes about three-quarters webbed, three phalanges free on toe 4; (11) tarsal fold absent; (12) skin densely tuberculate, particularly on limbs, less between eyes and center of back in females; tubercules conical with small keratinized spicules; (13) oblique row of tubercules present from posterior corner of parotoid glands to groin; (14) snout pointed with fleshy soft ridge extending to tip of snout; (15) iris golden.

This species is highly polymorphic. The coloration of the back can be uniformly brown to light gray, or with a variety of leaf-like patterns with successive shades of dark to light brown or gray. A whitish mid-dorsal stripe can occur and can be very thin to 5 mm wide. Flanks are generally darker than the back.
distribution: Primary forest of French Guiana. Probably occurring in Suriname and Brazil Amapa as well. Localities range from 20 to 170 m above sea level.
life_history:
During the rainy season (from November to January and from March to May), males call during daytime within 10 m of slowly running water. Calling males are usually isolated from each other and perched between 0.3 and 1 m high on a vine, dead trunk or root. The calls are long (several seconds) and composed of very short pulse groups that last for 30 ms. Pulse groups are spaced out by 97.2 ms and comprise 4.8 pulses / group on average. The peak frequency is 1.16 kHz and the pulses last 3.45 ms on average. Amplexus is axillary.

This species is likely not abundant.

comments:
Bayesian Inference and Maximum Likelihood analyses of 16S rRNA found that R. lilyrodriguezae is sister to the clade composed of R. chavin and R. yanachaga (Cusi et al. 2017).

This species was featured in News of the Week 7 October 2024:

We have known for decades now that the global protected area network leaves more amphibian species unprotected than it does for other terrestrial vertebrate classes. Given commitments by many countries to protect 30% of the earth by 2030, how might new protected areas (PAs) shore up these gaps? Steigerwald et al. 2024 used compiled range maps for terrestrial vertebrates and the World Database of Protected Areas to explore the amphibian conservation potential of microreserves (<10 km2), whose value is often discounted when considering more common conservation targets like mammal and bird species. They report the same proportion of unprotected amphibians as a comparable analysis 19 years ago, but that the rate of establishment of new amphibian-containing PAs has declined since the early 2000s. They also find that amphibian ranges are on average smaller than other terrestrial vertebrates, such that targeted microreserves could protect most of the range of many amphibian species—particularly threatened ones. Importantly, they find that microreserves increase the PA network’s coverage of amphibian diversity faster than larger PAs. This study demonstrates what we could gain by valuing targeted microreserves as a critically important conservation tool for underrepresented taxa. (Written by Emma Steigerwald)
common_name: Lily Rodriguez's Beaked Toad (English), Sapo picudo de Lily Rodriguezi (Spanish)
description:
Rhinella lilyrodriguezae is a large toad from the Rhinella festae species group, which was described from four adult females and two unsexed juveniles. The females have a snout-vent length range of 47.1 - 58.3 mm. The head is wider than long, but narrower than the body. In the dorsal view, the head is triangular with a long, acuminate, pointed, or rounded snout that protrudes over the lower jaw and has a slight antroventral angle. On the ventral side there is a keel on the snout. The small, round nostrils do not protrude, are directed laterally, and position near the anterior margin of the lower jaw. The area between the nostrils is concave. The distance from the tip of the snout to the nostrils is shorter than the distance from the nostrils to the eyes. In the profile, the canthus rostralis is angular and rounded, and continues along the head to above the eye, extending into the supratympanic crest. The loreal region is concave. The interorbital distance is twice the eye diameter. The upper eyelid has many low, keratin-tipped tubercles. The tympanum has a superficial membrane and a weakly defined annulus with a diameter that is smaller than the eye. The tympanum is isolated from the parotoid glands and post-orbital crest. The triangular parotoid glands are moderately large, about the same size as the eye diameter, and incorporated into a lateral row of tubercles that extended to the groin. The head has many crests, including the distinct orbital crest that begin as the canthus rostralis then runs above the eye and continue behind the eye as a the laterally expanded supratympanic crest. There are also moderately-developed cephalic crests. However there are no occiptial crests. The dorsal and lateral skin on the head has many warts. The skin on the rest of the dorsum has scattered conical tubercles with keratinized tips on otherwise smooth skin. The cloaca is positioned at the mid-level of the thighs and the opening is directed posteriorly. There is no cloacal sheath and the posterior half is free. The flanks have fewer tubercles. There is no dorsolateral fold. The skin on the throat, chest, and belly is granular. The dorsal skin on the forelimbs has densely scattered subconical tubercles. The forearm is long and slender, about a quarter of the snout-vent length. The hand is longer than the forearm. The distinct, round palmer tubercle is twice the size of the oval thenar tubercle. The palms also have indistinct, low supernumary tubercles. The long fingers have a relative length of I < II < IV < III and have basal webbing between fingers II - IV. Finger IV has well-defined lateral fringes. The tips of the fingers are rounded. The diffuse subarticular tubercles are low and round to oval in shape. The hind limbs are also long, slender, and have a spiculated dorsal surface like the forelimbs. The tibia is about 40% of the snout-vent length and is slightly longer than the foot. The foot does not have a tarsal fold but does have a large, elliptical inner metatarsal tubercle that is weakly protuberant and a smaller, round outer metatarsal tubercle that is half the size of the inner metatarsal tubercle. The feet also have indistinct supernumerary tubercles. The long toes have relative lengths of I < II < III < V < IV. They also have moderate webbing with a formula of I 1 – 2- II 1- – 2 III 1 – 3+ IV 3+ – 2 V, and all unwebbed portions have well-defined lateral fringes. The subarticular tubercles of the toes are similar to those found on the fingers: diffuse, low, and round to oval. The tips of the toes are also rounded (Cusi et al. 2017).

Rhinella lilyrodriguezae is physically similar to R. lindae, R. tenrec, and R. truebae, which are members of the R. acrolopha species group, in terms of size. But the species can be differentiated based on geography (the latter three are found in Colombia, and Panama), and by R. lilyrodriguezae having moderately developed cranial crests but lacking occiptal crests, an anteroventrally directed snout, a weak tympanic membrane, a dorsolateral row of small conical tubercles that connects the parotoid gland to the groin, basal webbing on the hands, and moderate webbing on the feet. Of the other Peruvian members of the R. festae species group (R. chavin, R. manu, R. nesiotes and R. yanachaga), which R. lilyrodriguezae is a member, most of the females are smaller than R. lilyrodriguezae, except R. chavin. Rhinella chavin can be differentiated by it having a rounded snout, relatively larger parotoid glands, glands on the limbs, and its dorsolateral row of tubercles only extending from the forearm insertion to the inguinal region. For all other comparisons, please see the citation (Cusi et al. 2017).

In life, the dorsum coloration varies based on time of day, with it being lighter at night than during the day. However it generally ranges from light brown to greenish brown and has irregular brown, dark brown or black markings. It may also have a grey white middorsal stripe. The flanks have irregular, dark green dorsolateral blotches that begin behind the parotoid glands and extend to the sacral region. The dorsolateral row of tubercles are dark brown. The chest, belly, and ventral thighs, are cream yellow to brownish grey, and has tiny light cream spots. The posterior region of the belly is cream yellow. The iris is silvery greenish with irregular black mottling (Cusi et al. 2017).

In preservative, the dorsum is light brown with irregular dark brown spots and markings on the dorsum and hind limbs. There are also dark gray transverse bands on the shanks. The flanks are cream colored and are marked with a well-defined, discontinuous, broad, black ventrolateral band that begins at the brown tympanum and ends in the inguinal region. The dorsolateral row of tubercles is reddish brown. The upper lip is cream colored and lacks bands or spots. The throat, chest, and belly become gray, but the minute light cream spots retain their coloration. The ventral surfaces of the thigh are the same as the ventral body. The palms and planters become dark gray while the subarticular tubercles become cream (Cusi et al. 2017).

There is considerable color variation within the same individual based on time of day, with the species being lighter at night than during the day. Between individuals, they may or may not have mid-dorsal stripes, and the "sharpness" of the snout may vary. Sexual dimorphism is unknown as no male specimens were found at the time of the species description. Developmentally, juveniles have more prominent cranial crests than adults (Cusi et al. 2017).
distribution: Known only from the type localities in montane forests of the Cordillera Azul National Park, Alto Biavo district, in northern Peru, between 1,245 and 1,280 m in elevation (Cusi et al. 2017).
life_history:
Rhinella lilyrodriguezae females were found during the dry season. The specimens were nocturnal and semiarboreal with all being found between 20:33 and 22:49 hours on bushes that were 10 - 100 cm from the ground (Cusi et al. 2017).

One gravid female was had 185 ovarian eggs with diameters between 3.2 - 2.7 mm. The eggs were pale cream yellow in preservative (Cusi et al. 2017).

Rhinella lilyrodriguezae can be found in sympatry with Pristimantis peruvianus, P. ventrimarmoratus, Osteocephalus mimeticus, and what are assumed to be Hyloscirtus phyllognathus, and Rulyrana flavopunctata (Cusi et al. 2017).
trends_and_threats: The area in which R. lilyrodriguezae is found has been impacted by logging, soil removal, and noise pollution. Subsistence game hunting and fishing by locals is also known in this area. However, at the time of the species description, the species had a recommended IUCN listing of "Data Deficient" (Cusi et al. 2017).
